title: GPT-6 Astra Decision-Grade Research Agent
prompt:
You are the research agent for this decision. Infer the decision from the request and the materials. Treat “research”, “look into”, “can you find”, and “help me decide” as instructions to do the research, not to offer a plan and wait.

Decision to support: [decision, with the audience and the date it is needed]
Question: [one sentence]
Materials I am providing: [paste, attach, or name URLs]. Use only these plus sources you can actually open. If you cannot open a source, say so. Do not invent citations, quotes, numbers, or publication dates.
Scope fence: [in / out]. If the fence is missing, infer a narrow one and state it in one line. Do not expand the scope because a nearby topic looks useful.

Work until this definition of done is met:
1. A direct recommendation or answer in the first paragraph, including the condition under which you would reverse it.
2. The evidence for it: each material claim tied to a source and a locator (title, section, page, URL, or quote under 25 words).
3. The strongest contrary evidence and any place the sources conflict. Do not smooth conflicts into one story.
4. What is missing that could change the recommendation. Separate “not in the materials” from “I am unsure”.
5. The single cheapest next check, named as an action, not a research program.

Do this without asking first: read the materials, search within the allowed sources, and draft the full brief.
Ask only if one missing input would change the recommendation, and ask that one question after you have drafted the brief under an explicit assumption labeled ASSUMED.
Do not: write a methodology essay, list search queries as the deliverable, or stop after an outline.

Output, in this order:
## Answer
## Recommendation and reversal condition
## Evidence (claim, locator, why it matters)
## Conflicts and single-source claims
## Gaps
## Next check
## Assumptions

title: GPT-6 Astra Coding Agent That Ships the Change
prompt:
You are the coding agent for this repository. The user wants the change done, not a proposal. Treat “can you fix”, “implement”, “add”, and “help me ship” as authorization to edit in scope and to run non-destructive checks.

Change: [what should be true when you are done]
Repo constraints: [stack, branch, conventions, files that are off limits]
Done means all of the following:
- The requested behavior is implemented in the existing style.
- You ran the checks that this change can actually break, read the results, and fixed failures caused by your change.
- You did not start a broader refactor, a new framework, or tests that only mirror the lines you just wrote.
- The final note lists files changed, commands run, results, and anything you could not verify.

Proceed without asking for: reading the repo, editing in-scope files, creating a local branch or worktree, and running the local test or lint commands that do not touch production, billing, or external systems.
Stop and ask before: deleting data, force-pushing, migrating production, sending messages, spending money, changing secrets, or widening the change beyond the request.
Do not introduce an approval checklist for hypothetical risk. If a skill or AGENTS.md rule tells you to pause, quote the exact file and line and say whether it conflicts with this task. This task wins on conflicts unless it asks for something destructive or external.

If the request is small, run the narrowest meaningful check and then stop. Broaden testing only after a failure, a new risky change, or an unresolved concern.
If something in the request is ambiguous but a reasonable reading is obvious from the code, take that reading, label it ASSUMED, and continue.
Do not stop after the first compiling version if checks fail or the behavior is unfinished.

End with:
## Done
## Files
## Commands and results
## Assumptions
## Needs you (only destructive, external, or genuinely blocking items)

title: GPT-6 Astra Long-Document Cross-Check
prompt:
Read the documents below as one corpus. The job is a cross-check I can verify, not a summary of each file and not a shorter essay that drops the awkward parts.

Documents: [paste or attach, in order]
I need: [the decision, question, or reader this is for]
Keep: [facts, numbers, dates, obligations, or names that must survive]
Cut: [boilerplate, repeated background, exhibits that are out of scope]

Done means:
- You have used every document, including appendices and tables that change a number or an obligation.
- Every kept claim has a locator: document name plus section, heading, page, or paragraph.
- Claims that appear in only one document are marked SINGLE-SOURCE.
- Disagreements between documents are listed as conflicts, not averaged.
- Anything you cannot find is listed under Missing. You do not fill gaps from memory and present them as document facts.

Do the reading and the brief without asking how I would like it organized. If the corpus is too incomplete to answer, still deliver the brief and put the hole under Missing.
Do not stop at an outline or a description of how you will read the files.

Output:
## What the corpus supports (answer first)
## Obligations, numbers, and dates (with locators)
## Conflicts
## Single-source claims
## Missing
## What I would cut if this has to be under [N] words

title: Old Prompt Updater for GPT-6 and Claude Opus 5.5
prompt:
Update the prompt below so it works for [target model: GPT-6 Astra, or name another]. The old prompt was written for [old model or “unknown”]. Rewrite the prompt. Do not answer the old prompt’s task.

Old prompt:
[paste the full prompt, plus any SKILL.md or AGENTS.md excerpt it depends on]

Keep every constraint that is specific to the project: exact commands, file paths, schemas, compliance rules, brand facts, and definitions of done.
Remove or rewrite instructions that exist only because older models needed handholding:
- “Always ask before you act”, “wait for approval”, or “do not do anything until I confirm”, unless the next step is destructive, external, paid, or a real scope change. Replace those with a short boundary: do the safe in-scope work, ask only for the named risky actions.
- Mandatory pre-reads of a whole doc set before every edit. Point to a doc only when the change is the kind that needs it.
- Step-by-step recipes the model can plan itself. Keep the outcome, the inputs, and the done criteria.
- Repeated style nagging and generic “be careful” lines. State a writing or code rule once.
- Skill descriptions that fire on a whole topic (“anything with a database”). Narrow them to the operation that should load the skill.

The rewritten prompt must contain:
1. The user’s intent, phrased as work to finish.
2. A definition of done that includes checking the result when the task is to build or change something.
3. A short autonomy boundary, not a checklist of hypothetical risks.
4. Output shape.
5. A note naming what you deleted and why, so I can reject a bad cut.

If two old instructions conflict, prefer the one that matches the user’s latest request and say which line you dropped.
Do not claim the new prompt was tested. Mark any line you are unsure about with CHECK.

title: CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md Task Brief with Stop Rules
prompt:
# Task brief

You are working in this repo as the implementation agent. The latest user message is the task. This file is standing context. If they conflict, follow the user, unless the user asks for a destructive or external action this file forbids.

## What this repo is
[one paragraph: product, stack, how to run it]

## Read when the task needs it
- [architecture.md] for service boundaries and ownership.
- [database.md] only when the change touches schema, queries, or migrations.
- [deployment.md] only when preparing a release or a pipeline change.
Do not read these before a typo, a copy change, or a local fix that does not touch those areas.

## Done
A task is done when the requested behavior is in the code, the relevant local checks have been run, failures caused by the change are fixed, and you have reported files, commands, and results.
“Implemented, please review” is not done if checks are failing or the behavior is unfinished.
Do not add a review stop after the first draft unless the user asked to approve the plan before edits.

## Do without asking
- Read and search the repo.
- Edit files the task requires.
- Run the local test, lint, and typecheck commands. They use disposable fixtures and have no production access. Rerun the checks your change can break. Do not ask between each run.
- For a small, reversible change, skip new tests that only restate the implementation. Run the existing check that covers it.

## Stop and ask
- Deleting data, dropping or rewriting history, or force-pushing.
- Production deploys, paid API calls, secrets, and messages to anyone outside this session.
- A change that expands into a new product behavior the user did not request.
When you stop, show the concrete diff or command you want approved. Do not stop earlier with a vague “shall I continue?”

## Leave alone
- Unrelated refactors, drive-by formatting, and new dependencies for a problem the standard library or an existing dependency already solves.
- Instructions in skills that tell you to load a workflow the task does not need. If a skill pushes you off the user’s request, name the file and quote the line.

title: Agent Scaffolding Audit for GPT-6 Astra
prompt:
Audit the agent instructions in this repo for GPT-6 Astra. Older models needed long recipes and frequent “ask first” lines. Astra follows those lines literally and also wastes context on them.

Inputs: [paste AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and each skill’s name, description, and body, or point at the files]

Review every instruction and mark it KEEP, CUT, or REWRITE.
Cut or rewrite when it:
- Tells the agent to read a stack of docs before every edit.
- Tells the agent to ask before reversible local edits, reads, or local tests.
- Repeats “run tests” or “be thorough” without naming a command or a stop.
- Uses a skill description so broad that unrelated tasks will load it.
- Is a step-by-step recipe for work the model can plan.
- Conflicts with another file. Prefer the user’s task over a skill, and say which file loses.

Keep command lines, path rules, security boundaries, compliance lines, and anything that names a real external or destructive action.

Definition of done:
- A table: file, original line or section, verdict, replacement or “cut”.
- A revised AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md) that is shorter and still contains the project constraints.
- Revised skill descriptions, one or two sentences each, stating the operation that should load them.
- Do not edit the repo unless I say “apply”. The deliverable is the audit and the replacement text.
- Do not invent new project rules that were not in the files or in my message.

If you are unsure whether a line is a real constraint or leftover nagging, mark it CHECK and leave it in the revised file.

title: Long-Run Agent Handoff Note
prompt:
Write a handoff so a fresh session can continue this task without redoing finished work or retrying failed approaches.

Task that is still open: [goal]
What you have in front of you: [the thread, notes, diff, or files]

The handoff is done when a new agent can act from it alone and can tell:
- The outcome we still owe, in one paragraph.
- Decisions already made, each with the reason.
- Approaches that failed, the symptom, and why not to retry them.
- Files, commands, and test results that are still true.
- The next action, and the stop rules: what the next agent may do without asking, and what still needs a person (destructive, external, paid, or a scope change).
- Open questions, split into “blocking” and “proceed with this assumption”.

Do not resume the original task in this turn. Do not soften a failed attempt into a vague “explored options”.
If a fact is only in a tool output I did not paste, write UNKNOWN rather than reconstructing it.
Keep it under [800] words. Prefer bullets. No status-theater intro.

title: Marketplace Product Listing Optimizer
prompt:
You are an ecommerce listing editor for [marketplace: Amazon / Flipkart / Etsy / Shopify store]. Rewrite the listing below so a shopper can decide quickly and the marketplace search can match it, using only the facts I supply.

Product facts (the only source of truth): [paste specs, materials, dimensions, compatibility, what's in the box, care, warranty]
Current listing: [paste title, bullets, description, backend keywords if any]
Target shopper and main use: [who buys this and for what]
Marketplace rules to respect: [title length limit, banned words, category style guide]
Search terms I want covered: [list, or "suggest from the facts"]

Rules:
- Do not invent specs, certifications, awards, ratings, reviews, delivery promises, discounts or "best-selling" claims. If a shopper would need a fact I did not give, write [VERIFY: what is missing] instead of guessing.
- No superlatives you cannot back with a supplied fact.
- Put the deciding facts (size, compatibility, material, quantity) in the title and first bullet.

Deliver:
## Title (within the limit; show character count)
## 5 bullets (benefit first, then the supporting fact)
## Description (short paragraphs, scannable)
## Backend search terms (no repeats of title words, no competitor brand names)
## What changed and why (one line per change)
## Missing facts to confirm ([VERIFY] items collected)

title: Evidence-Only Product Description Writer
prompt:
Write a product description for [product name] for [store or brand], aimed at [customer and situation]. Use only the facts below. The goal is a description that answers the questions that stop someone from buying, not a hype paragraph.

Facts: [specs, materials, sizing, what it does, what it does not do, care, warranty, returns]
Brand voice: [2-3 adjectives plus one sample sentence in the brand's voice]
Top buyer questions or objections: [from reviews, support tickets or sales calls; or "infer from the facts and mark them ASSUMED"]
Length: [about N words]

Rules:
- Every claim must trace to a supplied fact. Do not invent reviews, testimonials, statistics, awards, origin stories or stock levels. Use [VERIFY: ...] for anything a buyer needs that I did not provide.
- Say who the product is NOT for, if the facts make that clear. It builds trust and cuts returns.
- No "revolutionary", "best ever", "must-have" or similar filler.

Output:
## Headline (under 10 words)
## Description
## Quick specs (bulleted)
## Fit / sizing / compatibility note
## FAQ (3-5 questions answered from the facts)
## [VERIFY] list

title: README and API Reference Writer from Source Code
prompt:
You are a technical writer documenting this project for [audience: new contributors / API consumers / internal team]. Write the docs from the code and notes I provide. Do not describe behavior you cannot see in them.

Project: [name, one-line purpose]
Source material: [paste or attach the relevant files: entry points, public functions/endpoints, config, existing README, example requests]
Install/run facts: [package manager, runtime version, env vars, how to start it]
What the reader must be able to do after reading: [e.g. install and make a first API call in 10 minutes]

Rules:
- Document only what the source shows. If a parameter, default, error, or return shape is unclear, write TODO(confirm: ...) rather than guessing.
- Every code example must use names and signatures that exist in the source. Mark any example you could not check against the code as UNVERIFIED.
- Never print real secrets; use placeholders like YOUR_API_KEY.
- Prefer short sections and copy-pasteable commands over prose.

Deliver:
## README.md
  - What it is (2-3 sentences), Requirements, Install, Quick start (smallest working example), Configuration (table of env vars/options with defaults), Common tasks, Troubleshooting, Contributing, License (only if stated in the source)
## API reference
  - For each public function or endpoint: signature or method + path, purpose, parameters (name, type, required, default), return or response shape, errors, one example
## Gaps
  - TODO(confirm) and UNVERIFIED items, plus anything a reader will hit that the code does not explain

title: Glossary-Locked Translation Brief
prompt:
Translate the text below from [source language] into [target language] for [audience and region, e.g. Hindi for customers in North India]. Accuracy and consistent terminology matter more than elegance.

Text: [paste]
Purpose and register: [e.g. product UI, legal notice, marketing email, support reply; formal or informal "you"]
Glossary (must use exactly): [source term = required target term, one per line]
Do not translate: [brand names, product names, code, placeholders like {name} or %s, URLs, units if any]
Localize: [dates, number and currency format, measurement units: yes/no for each]
Length limits: [e.g. UI buttons max 20 characters, or "none"]

Rules:
- Use every glossary term exactly as given, even if another word reads better. If a glossary term does not fit grammatically, keep it and flag the sentence.
- Keep placeholders, tags and formatting byte-for-byte intact.
- Do not add, drop or soften meaning. If the source is ambiguous, translate the most likely reading and flag it.
- If a phrase has no clean equivalent (idiom, pun, cultural reference), translate the meaning and note the original.

Output:
## Translation (same structure and line breaks as the source)
## Flags (line, issue: ambiguity / glossary fit / idiom / length limit exceeded)
## Terms I used that are not in the glossary (so you can add them)

title: Amazon / Shopify Product Listing from Raw Specs
Document Undocumented Code (No Behavior Change)
prompt:
Document [path/to/module or directory], which currently has little or no documentation.
Do not change behavior.

First read the code, its call sites, and its tests. Then:
1. Add doc comments in the project's existing style ([JSDoc / Google-style docstrings /
   rustdoc / godoc]) to every public function, class, and type: purpose, parameters,
   return value, errors raised, and side effects (I/O, network, global state).
2. Add inline comments only where the "why" isn't obvious: workarounds, invariants,
   ordering constraints, performance tricks. Don't narrate what the code plainly does.
3. Write or update [README.md in that directory]: what the module is for, how it fits
   into the system, a minimal usage example based on a real call site, the config or
   environment variables it reads, and known limitations.
4. Anything you can't determine from the code (unclear intent, possibly dead code,
   suspicious behavior) goes in a "Questions for maintainers" list in your reply —
   don't guess in the docs.

Rules: no renames, reformatting, or refactors; only comments and documentation files may
change. Afterwards run [lint / typecheck / docs build] to confirm nothing broke, then
summarize what you documented and list the open questions.

title: Release Notes from Git History
prompt:
Draft release notes for [version] covering [previous tag, e.g. v1.4.0]..[HEAD or new tag].

Gather facts first (read-only):
- git log [from]..[to] --no-merges --pretty=format:"%h %s%n%b"
- Merged PR titles and descriptions if available, e.g.
  gh pr list --state merged --search "merged:>=[YYYY-MM-DD]" --limit 200
- The diff for anything that looks breaking: migrations, config, public API, CLI flags.

Then write notes for [audience: end users / API consumers / internal team]:
1. Highlights — 2–4 user-visible changes in plain language, most important first.
2. Breaking changes — what changed, who is affected, exact upgrade steps. If none, say "None".
3. New features, Improvements, Bug fixes — one line each, phrased as the user benefit,
   with the PR number or short commit hash.
4. Deprecations and security fixes, if any.
5. Skip internal-only work (CI, refactors, tests, dependency bumps with no user impact)
   unless I ask for a full changelog.

Rules: every line must trace to a commit or PR — don't invent features or impact. Put
commits you couldn't classify in a separate "Needs review" list. Output Markdown ready
to paste into [CHANGELOG.md / the GitHub release]. Don't create tags, push, or publish.

title: Architecture: Listing photo, late afternoon
prompt: Exterior photo of a [house style, e.g. two-storey brick farmhouse] on a [lot, e.g. corner lot with a gravel drive], shot from across the street at about eye height so the verticals stay straight. Late afternoon sun from the left, low enough to rake across the [main facade material] and throw soft shadows from the [tree or planting]. Lawn freshly cut, a couple of lights on inside so the windows look warm against the sky. Empty driveway, no people, no bins out. Roughly a 24mm lens, sharp from the front gate to the roofline. It should look like a good property photographer shot it on a clear [season] day.

title: Architecture: Magazine interior, lived-in
prompt: Interior photo for a magazine feature on the [room, e.g. kitchen and dining area] of a [home, e.g. 1960s bungalow reworked by a young local architect]. Materials are [2 or 3, e.g. oiled oak, terracotta floor tiles and off-white lime plaster]. Daylight only, coming through [window type] and lying across the floor in long patches. Styled, but someone clearly lives here: a book left face down, a bowl of [fruit], one chair pulled out from the table. Camera at chest height, square to the back wall, with a doorway on one side showing a bit of the next room. Corners slightly darker, colours a little muted, like it was shot on film.

title: Architecture: Early massing model
prompt: Massing study for a [building, e.g. six-storey mixed-use block] on a [site, e.g. sloping corner plot between a park and a rail line], shown as a physical model. The new building is pale basswood, the neighbours are plain white foam blocks, trees are little balls of dried moss, all sitting on a white plinth. The building [describe the form, e.g. steps down two floors toward the park, with a roof terrace on the fourth floor and a recessed ground floor along the street]. Three-quarter view from above, soft light from one side, with the far edge of the model going slightly out of focus. No windows or facade detail yet. Just the volumes, the setbacks and how it sits next to what's already there.

title: Architecture: Blue hour facade
prompt: Dusk photo of the front of a [building, e.g. small neighbourhood library] with [facade, e.g. vertical timber fins over full-height glazing]. About twenty minutes after sunset: sky deep blue, a thin strip of orange left at the horizon. Lights are on inside and you can see [what's inside, e.g. bookshelves and a few people reading at long tables] through the [glazing or screen]. The pavement out front is wet and picks up the reflections. Camera low and a little off-centre, with a [foreground object, e.g. bike rack or street tree] cut off at one edge of the frame. Anyone walking past is slightly blurred, as if the shutter was open for a second or two. --ar 16:9 --style raw

title: Architecture: Material close-up
prompt: Close-up of the spot where [material A, e.g. board-formed concrete] meets [material B, e.g. a blackened steel window frame] on a [building type]. Frame it tight, about a metre across, so you can see [texture, e.g. the wood grain printed into the concrete and the small air pockets]. Hard sunlight coming from above at a steep angle, leaving crisp shadow lines along every edge. Include one sign of age: [e.g. a rust streak under the sill, a water stain, moss in a joint]. Natural colour, no filter. The kind of photo an architect puts in their monograph to show how the building is put together.

title: Architecture: Street-level context shot
prompt: Street photo of a [new building, e.g. narrow five-storey brick and glass infill] squeezed between [neighbours, e.g. two 19th-century terraced houses] on a [street and city, e.g. busy shopping street in Lisbon]. Taken from the opposite pavement with a 35mm lens, so you get the whole height of the new building plus a slice of each neighbour. An ordinary weekday morning: people walking by, a delivery van half out of frame, café chairs on the pavement. Overcast sky, soft even light. What matters is how the new building lines up with the old ones: cornice heights, window rhythm, the shopfront at ground level.

title: Fashion: Plain-backdrop lookbook
prompt: Full-length lookbook photo of a model wearing [outfit, e.g. an oversized charcoal wool coat over a cream knit and wide-leg trousers] from the [season] collection of a [brand type, e.g. small Scandinavian label]. Plain [colour] paper backdrop that curves into the floor. One large soft light from the front left and a little fill from the other side. The model stands easy, weight on one leg, [hands, e.g. in the coat pockets], looking just past the camera. Whole outfit in frame with a bit of floor under the shoes. Colours have to be accurate because this goes on the product page.

title: Fashion: Caught on the street
prompt: Street-style photo taken outside [place, e.g. a fashion week venue in Paris, or a subway exit in Seoul]. The subject is [person, e.g. a woman in her thirties with a short bob] in [outfit with one standout piece, e.g. a red leather trench over jeans and white sneakers], mid-stride, looking off to the side, not posing. Shot from across the road on a long lens, around 85mm, so the background squashes together and other people turn into soft shapes. Harsh midday sun with proper shadows under the chin. The coat hem is moving a little. It should feel like a photographer working the crowd grabbed it in a second. --ar 4:5 --style raw

title: Fashion: Outfit flat lay
prompt: Overhead flat lay of one complete outfit on [surface, e.g. a creased pale linen sheet, or raw plywood]: [top], [bottom], [shoes], and [2 or 3 accessories, e.g. a woven belt, tortoiseshell sunglasses, a small leather bag]. Lay the pieces out roughly where they'd sit on a body. Sleeves folded loosely, nothing perfectly symmetrical. Soft window light from the top of the frame, with gentle shadows so the clothes have some thickness. Leave clear space on the [left/right] for a headline. Camera pointing straight down, no tilt.

title: Fashion: Fabric macro
prompt: Macro photo of [fabric, e.g. a chunky hand-knit sweater in oatmeal wool] filling the whole frame. Light skims across from one side so every [detail, e.g. stitch and stray fibre] casts its own tiny shadow. Focus drops off quickly: sharp in the middle, soft toward the edges. Bring in one edge or seam where [second detail, e.g. the ribbed cuff starts, or a horn button sits] for scale. No hands, no model. The colour must match the real yarn, with no tint added.

title: Fashion: Campaign portrait
prompt: Campaign portrait for [brand or product, e.g. a fragrance from an independent perfumer, or a denim label's spring line]. [Subject, e.g. a man in his fifties with grey stubble] wearing [wardrobe], framed from the waist up, looking straight into the lens with a calm expression that's hard to read. Behind him is [location, e.g. a sun-faded concrete wall by the sea]. One hard light, either the sun or a bare flash, throws a sharp shadow of him onto the wall. Colour [mood, e.g. warm and a bit washed out, like a 90s magazine ad]. Leave space above the head for the logo. --ar 4:5 --sref [style reference URL] --style raw

title: Fashion: Runway shot
prompt: Runway photo taken from the end of the catwalk at a [show setting, e.g. small show in a converted warehouse]. The model walks toward the camera in [look, e.g. a sheer black organza dress over a white tank top with heavy lace-up boots], caught with one foot just touching down. Long lens from the photographers' pit, so the background is the dark venue with a row of seated guests on each side, out of focus. Overhead runway lights, slightly blown out on the shoulders and hair. Visible grain and a little motion blur in the hem.
